<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
This is a well-designed follow-up. It closes the open questions from the nine-month report, adds an hours measure that doesn't depend on what staff choose to claim, registers the mediation analysis before the outcomes were known, and treats the Halden survivors as an upper bound rather than an estimate. The headline arithmetic checks out:
- Case-processing: 0.966/0.88 → +9.8% (timesheets) and 0.966/0.89 → +8.5% (logs).
- Halden: 96.8/86.6 → +11.8%, and 34.9/40.3 → −13.4%.
- Mediation shares sum to 100%.

Section 5's point about the meta-analysis is correct and important: four uncontrolled, scheduled-hours studies can't test for decay.

There are, however, two substantive problems with the new evidence. One is in the hours measure and the other in the mediation claim. I'll take them in order of importance.

## 1. The log-hours measure doesn't fit with the meetings result

The report describes system logs as "active log-in time on the county's case-management system," meaning time spent working on cases. But meetings happen off the system. Treated offices cut recurring meetings by about 3.3 hours a week relative to control (7.4 → 3.9, against 7.2 → 7.0), so on that description, log time should have fallen much *less* than total hours:

| Treated, relative to control | Hours per week |
|---|---|
| Total hours (timesheets, from a baseline of about 37.9) | about −4.5 |
| Meeting time | about −3.3 |
| Non-meeting time | about −1.2 (about −4%) |

The reported fall in log hours is −11%, which is close to the timesheet figure. Either logs capture something closer to total working time, meetings included, or the numbers don't add up.

This matters for the mediation analysis. If logs measure case time, then moving hours from meetings to casework increases log hours and output by roughly the same amount. Output per *log* hour would not rise unless each case hour became more efficient, for example through less fragmentation or fewer interruptions. That is a different mechanism from "removing low-value time," and it would make the 47% figure hard to interpret.

The report should state:
- what log-in time includes,
- baseline log *levels* alongside timesheet levels, and
- the arithmetic linking meeting time, log time and timesheet time.

Relatedly, "log data show slightly more work than timesheets" is inferred from percentage changes (−11% against −12%). Comparing changes says nothing about which measure records more work. That needs levels. And because logs miss off-system work, they aren't strictly the "stricter" measure.

## 2. The mediation test is pre-specified, but it isn't an independent confirmation

- **The test reuses the data that generated the hypothesis.** It was registered at month 11, after the nine-month results and the exploratory correlation were known, and it uses the same seven treated offices. Months 0–9 are inside the 24-month data. That makes it a pre-specified test on the hypothesis-generating sample, not a replication. "Survives a registered test" is accurate, but it doesn't fully answer Varga & Holm's objection. Their objection does now look overstated, but the report should acknowledge that this limit remains.
- **The inference needs to account for clustering.** "A larger sample of office-months" doesn't increase the effective sample size, which is still 14 offices. A CI of 28–66% on a mediation share from 7 v 7 clusters is narrow. Please confirm the inference accounts for clustering, using office-level bootstrap or randomisation inference rather than office-months treated as independent.
- **Meeting time may stand in for broader reorganisation.** Halden managers described cutting meetings alongside simplified approvals and less reporting. If Varden managers did the same, the "meetings" pathway picks up the effect of all those changes. The Limitations paragraph mentions unmeasured confounding in general terms, but this specific confounder deserves its own sentence.
- **The source of the baseline meeting data is unclear.** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. Baseline figures (7.4 and 7.2) now appear. Were they recovered from historical calendars? Say so, and say whether coverage was complete.
- **Mediator timing.** If meetings and fatigue were measured at the same points as the outcome, the analysis can't establish that changes in the mediators came first. The report should state the timing of measurement.

## 3. The Summary compares different measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." But 12.5% uses timesheets and 8.5% uses logs. The body correctly identifies 12.5% → 9.8% as the like-for-like comparison. The Summary should use that comparison, or report both.

Section 5's "declined by about a quarter" matches neither comparison. The fall is about a fifth on timesheets (2.7/12.5 ≈ 22%) and about a third if measures are mixed (4.0/12.5 = 32%).

The decline is also not tested. The two intervals (6.9–18.4 and 4.6–15.2) overlap heavily. "Consistent with some fading" is fair, but a formal test of the difference would help.

## 4. The control-office meeting audit affects the main estimate

Two of seven control offices reorganised in month 15. From that point on, the comparison group is partly treated with the mechanism under study, which pulls the 24-month DiD toward zero. The report should run a sensitivity analysis excluding those two offices, or excluding their post-month-15 data, for both the main estimate and the mediation analysis.

The audit also says something about the data. For the control average to move only from 7.2 to 7.0 while these two offices fell by about 2 hours, meeting time in the other five control offices must have *risen*. The report should check that this is right.

The interpretation of the audit itself is appropriately hedged. The open question it raises — whether reorganisation without an hours cut would capture the gain — is the right one for any future trial.

## 5. The Halden follow-up

- **Non-response.** Nine of the 23 organisations didn't respond, and non-response is probably related to outcome; reverted or struggling organisations may be less willing to report. Combined with the survivor selection the report already notes, the 14 are more selected than the text implies. The "upper bound" framing still holds, but non-response should be stated as an additional reason.
- **Hours baseline.** The 40.3 figure matches the 27-organisation baseline from Varga & Holm (the 17-organisation subset was 40.4). Please confirm that 40.3 is the baseline for these 11 organisations specifically, not a figure carried over from a different sample.
- **Reversion pattern.** A marketing agency reverted, citing client deadlines. Client-deadline work would usually be coded "discretionary," so this suggests the discretionary/coverage-bound distinction is a matter of degree. Coverage obligations can exist inside discretionary sectors. That's worth a sentence, given how much weight the earlier papers place on the binary.
- **Attrition disclosure.** R. Okafor is a Halden author. Varga & Holm showed that the working paper misdescribed when, and why, organisations withdrew. A follow-up co-authored from Halden is the natural place to acknowledge and correct that.

## Smaller points

- **Sick days.** If treated offices work fewer days, the −27% figure still needs to be expressed per scheduled day. This was raised for the nine-month report and remains open.
- **Resignations.** These still have no CIs.
- **Counter-arm costing.** The county's cost estimate (12% more staff → 9% higher cost per contact) implies staff are about 75% of cost. That's plausible, but it's the county's estimate, and the report should label it as such.
- **Characterising Varga & Holm.** They extrapolated *self-reported energy* to zero by month ten. They did not predict Varden's per-hour gain specifically. The rebuttal is fair, but it should describe their claim precisely.

## Overall

The main conclusions hold. The per-hour gain in case-processing has declined somewhat but remains clearly positive at 24 months under the strictest design available, and the meta-analysis's "no decay" claim was not supported. Before the meetings mechanism is treated as established, the report needs to:
- clarify what log time measures and reconcile it with the meeting data,
- account for clustering in the mediation inference,
- acknowledge that the test reuses the hypothesis-generating offices,
- run a sensitivity analysis excluding the two audited control offices, and
- fix the Summary's mixed-measure comparison.

I can draft revised Summary and Section 5 text if that would help.
